:::{.def}

[One GPU, used well](pt2_cluster.qmd), covers most research training. The honest cases for more: the epoch must finish faster, or the batch must be larger, than one GPU allows. The standard answer is **distributed data parallel (DDP)**: one copy of the model per GPU, each fed a different shard of the data, gradients averaged at every step.

This section turns our training script into a multi-GPU one. The loop itself does not change; five things around it do.

:::

## How DDP works

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false

flowchart TB
    classDef default color:#0081c2, stroke:#0081c2;
    D[(Batch)] --> S0[Shard 1]
    D --> S1[Shard 2]
    S0 --> F0[Forward + backward<br>on GPU 0]
    S1 --> F1[Forward + backward<br>on GPU 1]
    F0 --> G0[Local gradients]
    F1 --> G1[Local gradients]
    G0 & G1 --> A([All-reduce: average the gradients])
    A --> U0[Same update on GPU 0]
    A --> U1[Same update on GPU 1]
```

Every GPU holds an exact copy of the model. At each step, each copy computes gradients on its own shard of the batch; the gradients are averaged across GPUs; every GPU then applies the *same* update, so the copies never drift apart. The result is mathematically almost the same as training with one GPU and a batch N times larger — almost, because batch normalization statistics remain per-GPU.

The price is the averaging: an all-reduce across GPUs at every step. That communication is why two GPUs almost never halve the epoch time, and why small models sometimes run *slower* under DDP than on a single GPU: our 95,000-parameter CNN has steps so short that communication would dominate them. DDP pays off when the model is big enough to keep the GPUs busy between exchanges.

## The five changes

The complete script is `train_ddp.py`, next to this page's source in the course repository: `train.py` (the [single-GPU script](pt2_cluster.qmd)) plus the changes below. Everything else — the model, the schedule, the clipping, the early stopping — is untouched.

**1. A process group.** DDP runs as one *process per GPU*, and the processes must find each other. We let [`torchrun`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/elastic/run.html) create and launch them; it fills the environment variables we read:

```{.python}
local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])   # which GPU this process drives
rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])               # this process's global id
world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])   # number of processes

backend = "nccl" if torch.accelerator.is_available() else "gloo"
dist.init_process_group(backend=backend)     # find the other ranks
device = torch.device("cuda", local_rank) if torch.accelerator.is_available() \
    else torch.device("cpu")
```

- [NCCL](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl) is NVIDIA's communication library for GPUs; [gloo](https://github.com/facebookincubator/gloo) is its CPU counterpart. The fallback is also what lets you rehearse the mechanics without any GPU at all.

**2. Sharded data.** A `DistributedSampler` hands each rank a different shard of the dataset, padded so every rank gets the same number of samples:

```{.python}
sampler = DistributedSampler(train, shuffle=True, seed=42)
train_loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=64, sampler=sampler, ...)

for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
    sampler.set_epoch(epoch)  # reshuffle the shard assignment
    ...
```

The same seed on every rank keeps the shards disjoint. `set_epoch` gives each epoch a fresh assignment, the distributed counterpart of `shuffle=True` reshuffling [at every epoch](pt2_dataloaders.qmd). With `world_size=2` and 21,600 training images, each rank's loader yields 169 batches of 64: the effective batch of the run is 128, not 64.

**3. The wrapped model.** Forward passes go through the DDP wrapper; `backward()` through it triggers the gradient averaging:

```{.python}
model = Net().to(device)
ddp_model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank] if device.type == "cuda" else None)

loss = loss_fn(ddp_model(x), y)
loss.backward()   # DDP hooks in here: gradients are averaged across ranks
```

Clipping, the optimizer, and the scheduler keep operating on the plain `model`: its parameter tensors are the ones being updated, in place, on every rank.

**4. One rank with side effects.** Prints and checkpoints must happen exactly once, not once per GPU:

```{.python}
if rank == 0:
    print(f"epoch {epoch}  ...")
    torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), ...}, out)
```

**5. Reduced metrics.** Each rank only sees its own shard, so validation numbers must be combined before they mean anything. A sum-reduce over `[correct count, sample count]` (then a divide) gives the exact global accuracy:

```{.python}
def all_reduce_mean(value, device):
    t = torch.tensor([value], device=device)
    dist.all_reduce(t, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)
    return (t / dist.get_world_size()).item()
```

:::{.note}

Every rank runs the entire script — including `if rank == 0` blocks it skips. Keep the ranks' work identical except for the side effects: a `print` on all ranks is cosmetic noise, but a `torch.save` racing from several processes, or an early stop some ranks take and others miss, hangs the run at the next collective. Our script keeps even the early-stopping counters synchronized on every rank, and ends with `dist.barrier()` so no rank exits while others still expect it in a collective.

:::

## Launching

Locally, one node with two GPUs:

```{.bash}
$ torchrun --nproc-per-node 2 train_ddp.py --epochs 15
```

`torchrun` starts the two processes, sets the variables from change 1, and restarts the whole group if a process dies. And the rehearsal trick: on any machine, with no GPU in sight,

```{.bash}
$ torchrun --nproc-per-node 2 train_ddp.py --epochs 2 --max-batches 3 --cpu
```

```
torch 2.13.0+cu130  world size 2  backend gloo
epoch  1  train 2.308  val 2.277  acc 16.4%   5.3 s *
epoch  2  train 2.268  val 2.248  acc 25.0%   1.9 s *
```

Two processes on a laptop CPU: no speedup to measure, but every mechanism exercised — sharding, averaging, the single print line per epoch. The same run on GPUs is where the epoch time drops.

On a cluster, the same command goes into the batch script of the [previous section](pt2_cluster.qmd), with as many GPUs requested as processes launched:

```{.bash}
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8          # 2 ranks x 2 loaders x 2 workers each

uv run torchrun --nproc-per-node=$SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE train_ddp.py \
    --epochs 15 --data $SLURM_TMPDIR/data
```

`$SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE` is set by Slurm from the `--gres` line, so the same script serves a 2-GPU and an 8-GPU node. Multi-node jobs (several machines, one training) are the same idea with rendez-vous configuration; see the [PyTorch distributed docs](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html) when you get there.

## What to expect

- **Speedup under N.** With two GPUs, expect well under twice the throughput; communication grows with model size, and so does the *fraction* of time it hides. Measure: our baseline epoch [took seconds](pt2_loop.qmd), so run 2-3 epochs per configuration and compare.
- **The effective batch doubles.** Two ranks × 64 images is a batch of 128 for the optimizer. [The usual rule](pt2_dataloaders.qmd) — scale the learning rate with the batch — applies, or keep the effective batch fixed by halving each rank's batch size.
- **Per-GPU memory does not drop.** DDP replicates the model; every GPU holds the whole thing (weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations for its shard). When the model does not fit on one GPU, replication is the wrong strategy: that is [the next section](pt2_fsdp.qmd).
